---
title: "class imbalance"
---

## what counts as imbalanced

- a classification dataset is imbalanced when classes aren't represented roughly equally — e.g. 95% healthy / 5% disease
- mild imbalance (60/40) rarely needs special handling; severe imbalance (99/1, or rare-event detection like fraud) usually does
- imbalance is a property of the data, not of the model — it has to be addressed with how the data is used and how performance is judged, not just a different algorithm

## why it's a problem

- a model can achieve high accuracy by mostly or entirely predicting the majority class, without learning anything about the minority class — see [baseline models](baseline-models.qmd)
- many learning algorithms implicitly minimise overall error, so they're naturally biased toward getting the majority class right, since that's where most of the loss comes from
- standard threshold-based metrics and even roc/auc can look better than the model deserves under heavy imbalance — see [evaluation metrics](evaluation-metrics.qmd#roc-curve--auc)

## resampling approaches

::: {.table-responsive tabindex="0"}

| approach | how it works | tradeoff |
|---|---|---|
| random oversampling | duplicates minority-class examples | risks overfitting to the duplicated points |
| random undersampling | drops majority-class examples | discards data, can hurt if the majority class is also informative |
| smote | synthesises new minority examples by interpolating between existing ones | avoids exact duplicates, but can create unrealistic points in sparse regions |

:::

- resampling changes the training distribution, not the real-world distribution — evaluate on data that reflects the true class balance, not the resampled one

## algorithm-level approaches

- class weights: penalise mistakes on the minority class more heavily in the loss function, instead of changing the data (e.g. `class_weight="balanced"` in scikit-learn)
- threshold adjustment: many classifiers output a probability; moving the decision threshold away from 0.5 trades precision for recall (or vice versa) without retraining — read off the right threshold from a [precision-recall curve](evaluation-metrics.qmd#precision-recall-curve--average-precision)
- anomaly/novelty detection framings treat the minority class as "rare/abnormal" rather than as a standard classification target, when it's extremely rare

## evaluation under imbalance

- prefer precision, recall, f1, and the precision-recall curve over accuracy and roc/auc — see [evaluation metrics](evaluation-metrics.qmd)
- always report performance alongside the class balance it was measured on, and compare against the majority-class baseline
- stratify train/test and cross-validation splits so each fold preserves the original class proportions — see [train/test splits](train-test.qmd)

## practical considerations

- resample (or reweight) only the training fold, never the validation or test data — fit any resampling inside the cross-validation loop to avoid leakage, the same principle as [avoiding leakage in preprocessing](feature-engineering.qmd#avoiding-leakage)
- more data for the minority class (if obtainable) usually beats synthetic resampling of what's already there
- collecting better features that actually separate the classes often helps more than any resampling trick — imbalance handling can't manufacture signal that isn't in the data
